content: Grace Fernald was a prominent educational psychologist who made significant contributions to literacy education in the early 20th century. Born on November 29, 1879, in Clyde, Ohio, she spent her early years in New York and New Jersey before attending Mt. Holyoke and Bryn Mawr for college. In 1907, she earned her doctorate in psychology from the University of Chicago. By 1911, she had joined UCLA, where she eventually became the head of the Psychology Department and Laboratory at the State Normal School. It was at UCLA that her groundbreaking research into reading and writing processes gained widespread recognition. In 1921, Fernald established the first clinic for remedial instruction at UCLA. Her work was heavily influenced by tactile learning methods rooted in the ideas of Quintilian, Seguin, and Montessori. She developed a kinesthetic spelling and reading method that encouraged struggling students to trace words, integrating physical, auditory, verbal, and visual elements into the learning process. This approach, now known as multimodal learning or multisensory imagery, remains a cornerstone of modern special education and remedial reading instruction. Her research culminated in her 1943 publication, Remedial Techniques in Basic School Subjects, which solidified her legacy in the field. Fernald’s kinesthetic method was detailed in a foundational 1921 study published in the Journal of Educational Research. The study followed four boys who learned to spell and read using her method. The process involved five phases, beginning with students selecting focal words, tracing them on a chalkboard while repeating them aloud, and eventually writing them independently. Subsequent phases included creating sentences, reading isolated words from books, reading whole phrases, and finally engaging in silent reading. Over time, all four boys achieved grade-level reading proficiency, with some even surpassing expectations and becoming avid readers. Fernald and her collaborator, Keller, noted that the students demonstrated the ability to learn new words by analogy, a compensatory strategy still used in education today. They also emphasized the importance of individualized instruction and proper motivation, principles that continue to influence programs like Marie Clay’s Reading Recovery. Fernald’s career was celebrated upon her retirement in 1948 after 27 years at the UCLA clinic. Time magazine highlighted her work in an article titled “Reading by Touch,” which described her kinesthetic method and its success in helping students overcome reading difficulties. Fernald explained that such difficulties often stem from an inability to visualize the appearance of words. Her clinic required students to have average intelligence and parental commitment to the program, with remediation typically taking two months to two years to achieve grade-level reading proficiency. The impact of Fernald’s method extended beyond the classroom. A former student of her clinic recounted his experiences in a 1998 edition of the History of Reading News, describing sessions that included activities like finger painting. His mother also shared her perspective, emphasizing how Fernald’s work not only transformed her son’s academic abilities but also positively affected their entire family. These personal accounts highlight Fernald’s dedication and the profound influence of her teaching methods. Upon her death in 1950, Fernald’s peers lauded her contributions to education, particularly her development and direction of the UCLA clinical school. Her innovative approaches to literacy instruction and her commitment to helping struggling readers left an enduring legacy in the field of education.
